name: Flattop

card.summary: The flattop is a short haircut with a flat, upright top and tight sides that adds a squared, angular line to the head and jaw area.
card.note: Needs frequent barber visits to keep its shape.

quick.overview:
A flattop is a classic men's cut with short back and sides and a top that is cut flat and stands upright. The squared silhouette adds height at the crown and an angular, structured look to the head.

It was popular in the early and mid 20th century, associated with athletes, soldiers and astronauts, and still has dedicated wearers.
quick.how: Barbers do most of the work with clippers, using clipper-over-comb and freehand techniques on the top, then finish with shears. Wax, pomade, gel or hairspray help the top stand up.
quick.risks: No health risks. The shape grows out quickly, and wearers typically book cuts every two to three weeks. It needs enough hair density on top to stand up.

lead: A flattop is a hairstyle with short sides and back and a top cut flat and upright. It is considered a classic short male cut that was popular in the early and mid 20th century and keeps dedicated followers.[1]

For appearance, it creates a squared silhouette that adds height at the top of the head and emphasizes the angles of the jaw and head shape. Variants include the classic, a counterculture version with a longer top, the flattop with fenders, and the horseshoe flattop.[1]
Mid-century publications such as Life (1956) and Time (1959) covered the style, and butch wax was the product name tied to it in the 1950s.[1]

chain: Flat top cut over short tapered sides
Angular, structured head and jaw look
angle.text: The flat upright top adds apparent height and a geometric outline, which people choose to make the head look more angular and the jaw more prominent.

infobox: About 1/4 inch at crown, 3/4 to 1 1/4 inch front[1]
Cut every two to three weeks[1]

paras: The classic version is cut flat from front to back and rounded at the crown, with the top about a quarter inch at the crown and three-quarters to one and a quarter inches in front, and the back and sides around a quarter inch.[1] The counterculture variant leaves the top two or three inches in front, the flattop with fenders slicks long sides back into a ducktail, and the horseshoe flattop shaves the back and sides to the skin leaving a horseshoe-shaped top, often worn by U.S. soldiers.[1] Some versions show a strip of scalp at the center top, known as a landing strip.[1]

sections.h: How it is cut and kept
paras: Clippers do most of the work, with clipper-over-comb and freehand techniques on top and detachable blades on the back and sides; the upper sides are boxed in rather than contoured, and master barbers finish with shears in a move called the scissor salute.[1] Products include wax pomade, hairspray, mousse, gel and cream, and most wearers use a blow dryer.[1] Maintenance cuts are needed every two to three weeks, and some wearers go weekly, a habit barbers call Flattop Friday.[1]
Public figures pictured with flattops include Pierre Curie, Johnny Unitas, Walter Cunningham, H.R. Haldeman, Gene Kranz and Howie Long.[1]

timeline.event: Life publishes a piece on how to square flattop hair.[1]
